query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy, controlled thermal aging induces chemical short-range order (SRO) that localizes near grain boundaries, reducing local cohesion and thereby precipitating a transition to brittle failure during mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA produced via rapid quenching, exhibiting minimal intrinsic SRO.
generation.intervention: Thermal annealing at moderate temperatures (600–700°C for 1–10 hours) followed by slow cooling to promote SRO development, as compared to a rapid quench control.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing performed under cryogenic (and room temperature) conditions to probe toughness, complemented by microstructural analysis (TEM and atom probe tomography) to quantify SRO and its localization.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometric clusters of short-range order (SRO) forming preferentially at or near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment drives local chemical clustering (SRO) within the HEA matrix. These SRO clusters alter the grain-boundary chemical environment by reducing cohesion and acting as preferential crack nucleation sites under low-temperature loading, leading to a brittle response distinct from conventional alloy embrittlement mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples thermally aged to develop SRO will exhibit reduced fracture strain and lower toughness, with evidence of intergranular crack propagation, especially under cryogenic conditions, relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched single-phase alloy with minimal SRO formation and correspondingly higher ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under service conditions involving cryogenic to room temperatures in high-entropy alloys retaining an overall single-phase composition.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of SRO on toughness reduction is uncertain, and the subtlety of SRO effects may be influenced by secondary microstructural evolutions not fully controlled by the thermal treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA specimens: one set subjected to thermal annealing at 600–700°C for 1–10 hours with slow cooling to promote SRO, and a control set rapidly quenched to suppress SRO formation. Perform tensile tests at cryogenic and room temperatures, while characterizing the microstructure via TEM and atom probe tomography to quantify SRO presence and distribution.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of SRO clusters (size, distribution, and volume fraction) using atom probe tomography.
Tensile properties including fracture strain, toughness, and mode of fracture (intergranular versus transgranular) at both tested temperatures.
Comparison of crack initiation and propagation characteristics via in situ or post-mortem microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples with significant SRO exhibit fracture properties (fracture strain, toughness, and crack propagation mode) statistically indistinguishable from the rapidly quenched baseline, or if the fracture remains predominantly ductile, the hypothesis that SRO reduces grain-boundary cohesion and induces brittle behavior would be falsified.

proposals.intervention: Thermal treatment to induce controlled chemical short‐range order (SRO): compare samples subjected to moderate temperature annealing (e.g., 600–700°C for 1–10 hours, followed by slow cooling) versus rapid quenching to freeze the high-entropy state.
proposals.conditions: Tensile testing at cryogenic (and room) temperatures to evaluate toughness under low-temperature loading; microstructural characterization using TEM and atom probe tomography post-deformation.
proposals.structural_mediator: Emergence of nanometric SRO clusters, particularly near or at grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: In the HEA matrix, controlled thermal aging promotes local clustering of like elements (SRO) which subtly reduces grain-boundary cohesion. Under mechanical loading, these chemically altered interfaces become preferential sites for crack nucleation, leading to brittle failure—a mechanism distinct from conventional depletion-induced embrittlement.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with developed SRO will exhibit a marked reduction in toughness (e.g., lower fracture strain and enhanced intergranular crack propagation) compared to the rapidly quenched baseline, especially under cryogenic conditions. The effect will be absent or much less pronounced in the standard single-phase state.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests the hypothesis that even an initially single-phase HEA can develop a microstructural feature (SRO) that undermines toughness. The controlled comparison directly distinguishes HEA behavior—via SRO‐induced embrittlement—from conventional alloy segregation or intermetallic precipitation mechanisms.

proposals.material_system: Single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a minor Ti addition (to maintain high configurational entropy)
proposals.intervention: Thermal aging at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700°C for controlled durations) to potentially induce nanoscale precipitation at grain boundaries, while keeping the bulk composition complex.
proposals.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing (tensile and creep) in intermediate temperature regimes combined with in-depth microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS, TEM) post-aging.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially nucleated at grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: While HEAs typically resist deleterious intermetallic formation, a controlled minor addition and thermal exposure can drive subtle grain-boundary precipitation. This local phase separation weakens the cohesion at the interface and causes embrittlement under service-like loading, providing a mechanistic contrast to conventional alloys where larger precipitates are the primary culprit.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will show a transition from ductile to brittle fracture along grain boundaries during high-temperature testing, with measurable reductions in toughness and altered creep behavior compared to the unaged, single-phase baseline.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This research direction isolates a grain-boundary-specific mechanism in a compositionally complex alloy that is not predicted by conventional alloy models, thereby offering a controlled comparison (aged vs. unaged) to decisively test the hypothesis of micro-precipitation induced embrittlement.

proposals.intervention: High strain rate deformation experiments combined with in situ characterization (e.g., high-speed digital image correlation and TEM observations) to monitor dislocation activity and localized deformation.
proposals.conditions: Perform tensile and compression tests over a range of strain rates and temperatures (from cryogenic to moderate high temperatures) to simulate varying service conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Development of localized dislocation channels and strain localization adjacent to grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: The sluggish diffusion and complex energy landscape in refractory HEAs can promote inhomogeneous dislocation motion. Under high strain rates or at low temperatures, localized channels of intense deformation can form near grain boundaries, serving as precursors to microcrack nucleation and eventual brittle failure—an effect not usually seen in homogeneous conventional alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under conditions of high strain rate or low temperature, the alloy will demonstrate premature fracture with features of quasi-cleavage and localized damage zones, contrasted with more uniform plastic flow in the baseline single-phase state at moderate strain rates.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study provides a controlled mechanical test that directly links the microstructural evolution (localized dislocation channeling) to a transition from ductile to brittle failure in HEAs, challenging conventional expectations and identifying a distinctive mechanism operative in compositionally complex alloys.

proposals.intervention: Cyclic loading experiments with variable strain amplitudes to induce fatigue-associated damage, with systematic comparison between specimens subjected to sub-critical cyclic loading and monotonic loading.
proposals.conditions: Tests conducted at room and cryogenic temperatures with controlled cycle counts and amplitudes; subsequent microstructural evaluation using EBSD and TEM to detect nanoscale shear band formation.
proposals.structural_mediator: Accumulation of localized nanoscale shear bands at or near grain boundaries leading to decohesion.
proposals.mechanism: Repetitive cyclic loading in HEAs can promote shear band initiation along grain boundaries even in the absence of conventional segregation. The accumulation of these localized deformation zones gradually degrades the toughness of the alloy, providing a fatigue-induced embrittlement mechanism distinct from the typical grain-boundary precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: After a critical number of cycles at higher amplitudes, the alloy will exhibit a transition to brittle fracture modes marked by intergranular crack initiation associated with shear bands, as compared to the baseline monotonic deformation which retains higher toughness.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests whether cyclic, fatigue-induced damage in an initially single-phase HEA can produce brittleness through localized microstructural changes (shear band formation), thereby offering a controlled comparison against conventional alloy behavior under cyclic vs. monotonic loading.

critiques.addresses_problem: The direction directly targets the unknown mechanism of toughness degradation in single‐phase HEAs by linking localized dislocation channeling near grain boundaries under extreme loading conditions to brittle failure. This is well aligned with the research question.
critiques.constraints: The experiment uses a refractory HEA (HfNbTaTiZr) and tests across a wide temperature and strain‐rate range, thus respecting the constraint of retaining composition complexity while mimicking service conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis that sluggish diffusion promotes inhomogeneous dislocation motion leading to localized deformation is physically plausible in refractory HEAs, though the causal link between dislocation channeling and embrittlement must be clearly isolated.
critiques.feasibility: In situ high-speed digital image correlation combined with TEM is challenging but established. The controlled tensile and compression tests under variable conditions are feasible with current techniques.
critiques.evidence: No direct prior records are cited. However, similar in situ methodologies have been successfully applied in related studies.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the difficulty in conclusively linking observed dislocation channels to the onset of brittle failure rather than other deformation features or mechanisms.
critiques.fix: Integrate complementary local mechanical testing (such as nanoindentation or micro-pillar compression) to more directly correlate dislocation channel formation with microcrack nucleation at grain boundaries.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction tests whether controlled thermal aging can induce short-range order (SRO) that undermines grain-boundary cohesion, thus providing a direct mechanism for toughness degradation in an initially single-phase HEA.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraint by maintaining a single-phase, compositionally complex CoCrFeMnNi alloy and uses thermal treatments that are typical for such systems.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism that SRO alters local chemical environments to reduce grain-boundary cohesion is physically sound, though the degree of SRO and its mechanical impact may vary.
critiques.feasibility: The thermal treatments, tensile tests at cryogenic/room temperatures, and high-resolution characterization (TEM and APT) are well within current experimental capabilities.
critiques.evidence: While no specific literature records are cited, the formation of SRO in HEAs and its microstructural effects are supported by earlier observations in similar systems.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the subtlety of SRO effects; quantifying the extent to which SRO reduces toughness might be challenging and could be confounded by uncontrolled microstructural evolution.
critiques.fix: Incorporate quantitative atom probe tomography (APT) to precisely measure SRO extent and correlate these measurements with local mechanical properties to strengthen the causal evidence.

critiques.addresses_problem: While this approach investigates a grain-boundary mechanism (nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates) as a cause of embrittlement, it closely parallels known phenomena in conventional alloys and may not reveal a unique mechanism in HEAs.
critiques.constraints: The addition of a minor element (Ti) and subsequent thermal aging challenge the single-phase constraint as they intentionally induce phase separation, which risks mimicking conventional embrittlement mechanisms.
critiques.physical_soundness: The idea that controlled nanoscale precipitation could lead to localized embrittlement is physically plausible; however, it is not clearly distinct from conventional alloy behavior given that grain-boundary precipitation is well established as a brittleness mechanism.
critiques.feasibility: The experimental protocols (thermal aging, high-temperature mechanical tests, SEM/EDS, TEM) are standard and achievable.
critiques.evidence: Similar grain-boundary precipitation phenomena have been observed in both conventional and some complex alloys; the records do not decisively support the uniqueness of this mechanism in HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The risk lies in the possibility that the mechanism investigated might not be unique to HEAs and therefore may simply recapitulate conventional precipitation-induced embrittlement, failing to address the specific open question.
critiques.fix: Refine the thermal aging parameters to ensure that any precipitates remain nanoscale and uniquely influenced by the high configurational entropy of HEAs, and include additional characterization to distinguish these precipitates from those in conventional alloys.

critiques.addresses_problem: The approach examines whether cyclic loading induces fatigue damage via nanoscale shear band formation at grain boundaries, which could lead to embrittlement—a mechanism that differs from conventional segregation or precipitation.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraints by maintaining a single-phase equiatomic HEA and compares cyclic loading against monotonic loading under controlled temperature conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: While fatigue-induced shear banding is a recognized phenomenon, attributing it as a unique embrittlement mechanism in HEAs (distinct from conventional fatigue behavior) requires careful isolation of variables.
critiques.feasibility: Cyclic mechanical testing with detailed microstructural evaluation (using EBSD and TEM) is feasible, although differentiating fatigue-related damage from other cyclic phenomena may be technically challenging.
critiques.evidence: There is literature on fatigue behavior and shear band formation in various systems, but no specific prior records conclusively support this unique mechanism in single-phase HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that fatigue-induced damage (shear bands) is a common response in many alloys under cyclic loading, so it may be hard to attribute observed embrittlement as a distinct HEA phenomenon.
critiques.fix: Design the experiments to include a comparative analysis with conventional alloys under identical cyclic conditions to clearly demonstrate that the shear band-induced embrittlement mechanism is enhanced or uniquely active in HEAs.
